metadata.title: Pull Your Arms In and You Spin Faster — But Where Did the Energy Come From?
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: A spinning skater pulls her arms in and spins faster. Where does the extra energy come from?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: A skater spins on the tip of her skate with her arms stretched out. The ice exerts almost no torque on her, so nothing outside can speed her up. Yet when she pulls her arms in, she spins far faster. Where does that extra rotational energy come from?
beats.new_visual_element: Top-down skater (teal dress, skin-tone arms and head, dark hair bun) rotating slowly counterclockwise with arms extended; hands trace a light dashed circle; label 'no external torque' at the top.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: slowly spinning skater, dashed hand circle, label

beats.narration_text: The quantity that cannot change is her angular momentum. For rotation about a fixed axis, L equals I omega. The moment of inertia, I, depends on how far her mass sits from the axis, and it grows with the square of that distance. With no external torque, L stays exactly the same.
beats.new_visual_element: Crimson radius arrow from the axis to one hand, labeled r. Equation card L = I omega, with a note that L points out of the page for a counterclockwise spin.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: spinning skater, radius arrow r, equation card L = I omega (stays to the end)

beats.narration_text: Now she pulls her arms in. Her moment of inertia drops. Because the product I omega must stay fixed, omega must rise by exactly the factor by which I fell. Her spin speeds up on its own.
beats.new_visual_element: Arms shorten while the spin rate increases on the same interpolator; the radius arrow contracts. Two bars beside the card: I shrinks, omega grows, and the product L stays level (check mark).
beats.accumulated_scene_state: fast-spinning skater with arms in, short radius arrow, I bar low, omega bar high, L constant

beats.narration_text: Now track her energy. Rotational kinetic energy is one half I omega squared, which equals L squared over two I. With L fixed and I smaller, the kinetic energy grows by the same factor. That energy is not free. Each hand tends to keep moving in a straight line, so she must pull it inward, and the work her muscles do is exactly the kinetic energy she gains.
beats.new_visual_element: She extends her arms again and pulls them in a second time. A gold kinetic-energy bar grows in lockstep with the arm collapse; ink arrows on both hands point inward toward the axis, labeled 'muscle work'.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: fast-spinning skater, KE bar full, inward work arrows, equation card with K = L^2 / 2I

beats.narration_text: Angular momentum stays fixed throughout. Pulling in lowers I and raises omega in exact proportion, and the extra kinetic energy is paid for by the work of her own muscles, not created from nothing.
beats.new_visual_element: Final frame: skater spinning fast with arms in, KE bar full; three labels: L = I omega constant; I down, omega up; extra K = muscle work.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: final held frame with three summary labels
